learn.hook: One country, many governments, the same citizens — and yet no chaos. How? Welcome to federalism!
points: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and its various constituent units (like states or provinces).

In a unitary system there is only one level of government, or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government, which can pass orders to them. Sri Lanka remains a unitary system, while Belgium became federal in 1993.

Key features: (1) two or more levels (tiers) of government; (2) each tier governs the same citizens but has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration; (3) these jurisdictions are written in the constitution, so each tier's existence and authority are constitutionally guaranteed.

(4) Fundamental provisions of the constitution cannot be changed by one level alone — both levels must agree; (5) courts interpret the constitution and the powers of each level, and the highest court acts as umpire in disputes; (6) sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified.
Dual objective: to safeguard and promote the unity of the country, and at the same time to accommodate regional diversity. Mutual trust and agreement to live together are needed for it to work.

example.q: Think it through: In Country X, the national government can dissolve a province's government whenever it likes and take away its powers by a simple order. Is Country X federal?
steps: In a federation, each level's powers are guaranteed by the constitution.
One level cannot alone change or take away the powers of the other.
Here the provinces depend entirely on the national government's orders, so they are subordinate.
example.answer: No. Country X is unitary in practice, because its provinces are subordinate to the Centre.

learn.reallife: Your school has a principal for the whole school and a class teacher for each class. Both guide the same students, but each has fixed duties — a little like levels in a federation.

games.title: Federal or not? True or false
items: In a federation, different tiers of government govern the same citizens.
Each tier governs the same people, but on different matters.
In a unitary system, the central government can pass orders to the provincial or local government.
Sub-units in a unitary system are subordinate to the Centre.
In a federation, the central government can change the powers of the states on its own.
Fundamental provisions can be changed only with the consent of both levels.
Sources of revenue for each level of government are clearly specified in a federation.
This ensures each level's financial autonomy.
Federalism aims only at unity and ignores regional diversity.
It has a dual objective: unity of the country and accommodation of regional diversity.
In a federation, courts act as umpire if disputes arise between levels of government.
The highest court interprets the constitution and the powers of each level.

quiz.q: What is federalism?
options: A system where all power lies with one central government
A system where power is divided between a central authority and its constituent units
A system where the army runs the government
A system where only local governments exist
quiz.explain: In federalism power is divided between the Centre and units such as states or provinces.
quiz.mistake: Confuses federal with unitary government

quiz.q: Which of these describes a UNITARY system?
options: Sub-units are subordinate to the central government
Each level's powers are guaranteed by the constitution
Courts act as umpire between levels
Both levels must agree to change the constitution
quiz.explain: In a unitary system there is either one level, or the sub-units are subordinate to the Centre.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any country with states is federal

quiz.q: How can the fundamental provisions of a federal constitution be changed?
options: Only with the consent of both levels of government
quiz.explain: No single level can unilaterally change the basic provisions; both levels must agree.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the Centre is supreme in every federation

quiz.q: Who acts as an umpire if disputes arise between levels of government in a federation?
quiz.explain: Courts interpret the constitution and the powers of each level; the highest court acts as umpire.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the executive settles federal disputes

quiz.q: What is the dual objective of a federal system?
options: Safeguard national unity and accommodate regional diversity
Collect more taxes and spend less
Make the Centre strong and the states weak
Hold elections and end political parties
quiz.explain: Federalism aims to keep the country united while respecting regional diversity.
quiz.mistake: Sees federalism only as a way to divide power, not as a balance of unity and diversity

quiz.q: Which country shifted from a unitary to a federal form of government in 1993?
quiz.explain: Belgium became federal in 1993, while Sri Lanka remains essentially unitary.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Belgium and Sri Lanka cases

quiz.q: In a federation, each tier of government has its own jurisdiction in which matters?
options: Specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration
quiz.explain: Each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only one tier can make laws and levy taxes

quiz.q: Why are the jurisdictions of each level written in the constitution in a federation?
options: So that the Centre can change them easily
So that courts have no role
So that only one level can collect taxes
So that the existence and authority of each tier are constitutionally guaranteed
quiz.explain: Writing them in the constitution protects each level's powers from being taken away by the other.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the constitution as a guarantee of each tier's powers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What makes a country federal and not unitary? Tell me the key features!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Many levels, powers fixed by the constitution, courts as umpire — that's federalism!
teach.nudge: Good try! Where are each level's powers written, and who settles disputes between levels?

learn.hook: India's Constitution never uses the word 'federation' — yet India is federal. Let's find the proof!
points: Coming together federations: independent states come together to form a bigger unit, and the units usually have equal power (USA, Switzerland, Australia). Holding together federations: a large country divides power between the Centre and the states; the Centre tends to be stronger and units may have unequal powers (India, Spain, Belgium).
The Constitution declared India a Union of States. Originally there were two tiers — Union and states; later a third tier of panchayats and municipalities was added.

Three lists: Union List (national importance: defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency); State List (local importance: police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation); Concurrent List (both: education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession). If laws conflict on a Concurrent subject, the Union law prevails.

Residuary subjects (not in any list, like computer software) are for the Union government. Union Territories, such as Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi, do not have the powers of a state; the Central government has special powers in running them.

Changing the power-sharing arrangement is not easy: an amendment must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states. The judiciary (High Courts and Supreme Court) settles disputes over division of powers.

example.q: Think it through: A law on 'computer software' is needed. It is not in any of the three lists. Who can make it?
steps: Subjects not mentioned in any list are called residuary subjects.
The Constitution gives the Union government power to legislate on residuary subjects.
Computer software came up after the Constitution was made, so it is residuary.
example.answer: The Union government (Parliament) can make the law.

learn.reallife: Your local police station is run by the state government, while your passport is issued by the Union government — that is the Union and State Lists at work.

games.title: Which list?
items: Defence
Currency
Foreign affairs
Police
Agriculture
Irrigation
Education
Forest
Marriage and adoption
Trade unions

items.text: The USA, Switzerland and Australia are ___ together federations.
India, Spain and Belgium are ___ together federations.
In a coming together federation, the constituent states usually have ___ power.
In a holding together federation, the central government tends to be ___ powerful than the states.

quiz.q: India is an example of which type of federation?
quiz.explain: India is a large country that divided power between the Centre and the states — a holding together federation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks India was formed by independent countries joining together

quiz.q: Which subject is in the Union List?
quiz.explain: Defence is of national importance, so it is in the Union List. Police and agriculture are State subjects; education is Concurrent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks police, being about security, must be a Union subject

quiz.q: Education, forest and trade unions are subjects of which list?
quiz.explain: Both the Union and state governments can make laws on Concurrent List subjects like these.
quiz.mistake: Thinks education belongs only to the states

quiz.q: If a Union law and a state law conflict on a Concurrent List subject, which prevails?
quiz.explain: On Concurrent subjects, the law made by the Union government prevails in case of conflict.
quiz.mistake: Believes the earlier law always wins

quiz.q: Who has the power to make laws on residuary subjects such as computer software?
quiz.explain: Residuary subjects are not in any list, and the Constitution gives power over them to the Union government.
quiz.mistake: Assumes new subjects automatically go to the states

quiz.q: To change the power-sharing arrangement between the Union and states, an amendment must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority and then:
options: Ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states
Approved by a referendum of all citizens
quiz.explain: Both levels must agree: Parliament with a two-thirds majority, then at least half of the state legislatures.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Parliament alone can change federal provisions

quiz.q: Which of these is a Union Territory?
quiz.explain: Lakshadweep is a Union Territory; the Central government has special powers in running it. Kerala, Punjab and Assam are states.
quiz.mistake: Confuses small states with Union Territories

quiz.q: Which country is an example of a 'coming together' federation?
quiz.explain: In the USA independent states came together to form a bigger unit.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two routes to federation

teach.ask: Gappu tweets: 'How is power divided between the Union and the states in India? Explain the lists!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Union List, State List, Concurrent List and residuary powers — India's federal puzzle solved!
teach.nudge: Nice! Can you name the three lists with one example each? And who decides residuary subjects?

topics.title: How federalism is practised in India

learn.hook: A good constitution is a recipe — but the taste depends on how it is cooked. How has India actually practised federalism?
points: Linguistic states: after 1947 the boundaries of many old states were changed and new states created so that people speaking the same language lived in the same state. Some states were formed on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography, like Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand.
Some leaders feared linguistic states would lead to disintegration, but experience shows they made the country more united and administration easier.

Language policy: our Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, but it is the mother tongue of only about 40% of Indians. Besides Hindi, 21 other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages (22 in all).

English was to stop being used for official purposes in 1965, but many non-Hindi-speaking states demanded that it continue. The Central government agreed to continue English along with Hindi for official purposes.

Centre-state relations: for a long time the same party ruled at the Centre and in most states, and the Centre sometimes misused the Constitution to dismiss state governments. After 1990, regional parties grew and coalition governments at the Centre became common, building a culture of power sharing and respect for state autonomy. A Supreme Court judgment also made it difficult to dismiss state governments arbitrarily.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the Central government not force Hindi on non-Hindi-speaking states?
steps: India has great linguistic diversity; Hindi is the mother tongue of only about 40% of people.
Imposing one language could have alienated other language groups, as happened in Sri Lanka.
A flexible, accommodating policy kept trust between the Centre and the states.
example.answer: Because accommodating all languages strengthens unity, while imposing one could have caused conflict.

learn.reallife: A candidate can write the exam for a Central government job in any of the Scheduled Languages — a real sign of India's respect for language diversity.

games.title: True or false: federalism in practice
items: The Constitution of India makes Hindi the national language.
No language has been given the status of national language; Hindi is the official language.
There are 22 Scheduled Languages, including Hindi.
Besides Hindi, 21 other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages.
Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography.
Not all states were formed only on the basis of language.
Linguistic states have weakened the unity of India.
Experience shows linguistic states made the country more united.
After 1990, coalition governments at the Centre led to more respect for the autonomy of states.
Regional parties gained a role at the Centre, encouraging power sharing.
Hindi is the mother tongue of about 90% of Indians.

items.q: Official language identified by the Constitution
Year English was originally to stop being used officially
Language used along with Hindi for official purposes
After which year did coalition governments become common at the Centre?
Mother tongue share of Hindi, as a percentage (about)

quiz.q: On what basis were many new states created in India after 1947?
options: Size of the army in the region
quiz.explain: States were reorganised so that people speaking the same language lived in the same state.
quiz.mistake: Assumes states were drawn on religious lines

quiz.q: Which of these states was created on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography rather than language alone?
quiz.explain: Jharkhand, like Nagaland and Uttarakhand, was formed on such grounds. The others are Union Territories, not states.
quiz.mistake: Does not distinguish states from Union Territories

quiz.q: How many languages, including Hindi, are recognised as Scheduled Languages by the Constitution?
quiz.explain: Hindi plus 21 other languages make 22 Scheduled Languages.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to count Hindi along with the 21 others

quiz.q: What status does Hindi have under the Constitution?
quiz.explain: Hindi was identified as the official language; the Constitution did not give any language the status of national language.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'official language' with 'national language'

quiz.q: Why did the Central government agree to continue using English along with Hindi for official purposes?
options: English is the mother tongue of most Indians
quiz.explain: Non-Hindi-speaking states wanted English to continue, and the Centre accommodated this demand.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the decision was about English being widely spoken as a mother tongue

quiz.q: What change in Centre-state relations came after 1990?
options: The Centre began dismissing more state governments
Regional parties grew and coalition governments built respect for state autonomy
quiz.explain: The rise of regional parties and coalition governments at the Centre led to a new culture of power sharing.
quiz.mistake: Assumes federal relations only became more centralised over time

quiz.q: What was the outcome of creating linguistic states, according to experience?
options: The country became more united and administration became easier
quiz.explain: Fears of disintegration proved wrong; linguistic states strengthened unity.
quiz.mistake: Believes accepting diversity weakens unity

quiz.q: Before 1990, how did the Central government sometimes undermine the power of the states?
options: By making them Union Territories overnight
By refusing to hold Lok Sabha elections
By misusing the Constitution to dismiss state governments ruled by rival parties
quiz.explain: The Centre at times dismissed state governments controlled by rival parties, which went against the spirit of federalism.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the main problem in early Centre-state relations

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'India has so many languages! How did federalism handle states and languages without fights?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Linguistic states, no forced national language and coalition-era respect — India adjusts to stay united!
teach.nudge: Good! Does India have a national language? And how did coalition governments change Centre-state relations?

learn.hook: Who knows best where your village needs a new handpump? Not someone far away in the state capital — but people right there!
points: Decentralisation means taking power away from the Central and state governments and giving it to local government. The basic idea: many problems are best settled locally, and people can participate directly in decisions.
A major step came in 1992, when the Constitution was amended to make the third tier more powerful and effective.

Key provisions: regular elections to local bodies are compulsory; seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes; at least one-third of all positions are reserved for women; each state has a State Election Commission to conduct panchayat and municipal elections; state governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.

Rural local government (panchayati raj): a gram panchayat has ward members (panch) and a president (sarpanch), elected by the adult population, and works under the gram sabha (all the voters of the village). Panchayats are grouped into a panchayat samiti (block or mandal), and all panchayat samitis in a district form the zilla parishad, whose chairperson is its political head.

Urban local government: municipalities in towns and municipal corporations in big cities. The municipal chairperson heads a municipality; the mayor heads a municipal corporation. Challenges remain: gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most states have not given significant powers and resources to local bodies.

example.q: Think it through: A gram panchayat wants to repair the village pond. Who must approve its annual budget and review its work?
steps: The gram panchayat works under the overall supervision of the gram sabha.
The gram sabha consists of all the voters of the village.
It meets at least twice or thrice a year to approve the budget and review the panchayat's performance.
example.answer: The gram sabha — all the voters of the village.

learn.reallife: When your town elects ward councillors and your city has a mayor, or your grandparents' village elects a sarpanch, you are seeing decentralisation.

games.title: Rural local government: smallest to largest
games.prompt: Arrange from the village level up to the district level
items: Gram panchayat (village)
Panchayat samiti (block or mandal)
Zilla parishad (district)

quiz.q: What is decentralisation?
options: Giving all power to the Central government
Taking power from the Central and state governments and giving it to local government
quiz.explain: Decentralisation transfers power downward to local governments like panchayats and municipalities.
quiz.mistake: Confuses decentralisation with centralisation

quiz.q: In which year was the Constitution amended to make local government more powerful?
quiz.explain: The 1992 amendment made the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective.
quiz.mistake: Picks the year the Constitution came into force instead

quiz.q: At least what fraction of all positions in local bodies are reserved for women?
quiz.explain: At least one-third of all positions in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the one-third reservation with the two-thirds majority needed for amendments

quiz.q: Who conducts panchayat and municipal elections?
quiz.explain: Each state has an independent State Election Commission to conduct local body elections.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Election Commission of India conducts local elections too

quiz.q: Who is the president of a gram panchayat?
quiz.explain: The sarpanch is the elected president of the gram panchayat; the mayor heads a municipal corporation.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rural and urban local government heads

quiz.q: What is a gram sabha?
options: A meeting of all sarpanches of a state
All the voters of the village
quiz.explain: The gram sabha consists of all voters of the village and supervises the gram panchayat.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the gram sabha with the gram panchayat

quiz.q: All the panchayat samitis in a district together form the:
quiz.explain: The zilla parishad is the district-level body formed by all panchayat samitis of that district.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the three-level structure of panchayati raj

quiz.q: Which is a real difficulty that local governments still face?
options: They cannot have any elected members
Women are not allowed to contest
They have no elections at all
Gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most states have not given them enough powers and resources
quiz.explain: Despite the 1992 amendment, many local bodies lack regular gram sabhas and adequate powers and funds.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the 1992 amendment solved every problem of local government

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'Why should villages and towns run their own affairs? What did the 1992 change do?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Power to the people next door — panchayats, municipalities, regular elections and seats for women!
teach.nudge: Good! What did the 1992 amendment make compulsory, and what share of positions is reserved for women?
